extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and practitioners of scientific method and natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating analogy and exceptions in science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using analogical reasoning in scientific inquiry and for classifying and treating exceptional phenomena or apparent counterexamples to laws. Covers when analogy aids discovery, how it may mislead, and how to investigate and categorise exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy to generate discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy (the alliance between different domains, e.g., geometry and algebra) is a chief source of discoveries and facilitates apprehension of new methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Newton's geometric fluxions aiding calculus; Lagrange's view that uniting algebra and geometry lent mutual strength; Boole's algebraic approach to logic. Analogy is a productive heuristic for finding structural correspondences across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make allowances for differences when transferring analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: In making inferences from one kind of medium or domain to another, we must make allowance for difference of circumstances (mutatis mutandis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ocean waves vs sound vs light differ in velocity and vibration character; do not expect close outward resemblance even when principles (harmonic motion) are shared. Always identify and adjust for differing conditions (e.g., transverse vs longitudinal vibrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat analogical inferences as provisional and verify by observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical arguments are valuable especially when direct evidence is limited, but they must be compared with observation and experiment and not accepted from preconceived theory alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cautionary example: Newton entertained undulatory ideas but his preconceived theory about rays misled him because he did not sufficiently compare with observation (diffraction/interference). Use empirical tests to confirm analogical hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit analogical extrapolation as similarity decreases
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability and force of an analogical argument decrease rapidly as the condition of the object under consideration diverges from the case used in the analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculation about life on other planets is tolerated only insofar as conditions (temperature, atmosphere, chemistry) are analogous; avoid speculative overreach when dissimilarities are large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize possible outcomes when analogy appears to fail
rubrics_metrics.description: When analogy seems to fail, three results are possible: (1) the analogous feature exists; (2) it seems not to exist but really does (apparent failure); (3) it really does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether failure is due to perceptual limits or disguised phenomena (e.g., diffraction makes light 'bend' only subtly), before concluding true non-existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: State scientific laws with precise scope and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every law of nature must be stated with the utmost generality of all the instances really coming under it; if exceptions exist the statement without allusion to them is erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: do not say 'All liquids expand by heat' if water below 4°C does not; instead specify the class or mention exceptions explicitly. 'General' should mean true of an assigned class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate universal principles from general (non-universal) principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between universal principles (no exceptions) and general principles that are more frequently obeyed than violated; in scientific view, general principles must be universal with respect to some distinct class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Babbage's distinction cited; ensure that general statements in science define the class they apply to, otherwise they are not genuine principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: First inquiry for a supposed exception: is the fact real?
rubrics_metrics.description: When a supposed exception to a law is brought forward, the first proper inquiry is whether there is any breach of the law at all — i.e., whether the supposed exceptional fact is actually a fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the source of the assertion and the observer's conditions; many apparent exceptions are false assertions or misperceptions (e.g., Royal Society investigating the King's fish/bucket claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test alleged counterexamples experimentally with suitable precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterclaims or objections should be tested by trial and precise observation, taking appropriate precautions to avoid misleading results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: the Copernican objection that a dropped stone would fall behind; careful experiment (or analysis by laws of motion) shows the assertion false or reveals small detectable deflection (Benzenberg). Use accurate tests to resolve disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate genuine contradictory facts from those explainable by other causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When exceptions appear, exercise judgment to assign to them their proper place: some may be insuperable contradictions, others may be results of different causes or disguised manifestations of the same law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance or rejection of a theory depends on discriminating the single insuperable contradictory fact from many that can be reconciled; investigate alternative causes and interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware pseudo-objects created by language or symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical and symbolic use of language and mathematics can produce conceptions of things which do not exist (e.g., negative square root as a 'meaningless' sign without analogous meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when mathematical symbols represent formal signs rather than physical realities; avoid confounding symbolic convenience with ontological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional phenomena are valuable raw material for discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Strange and inexplicable facts commonly lead to novel and important discoveries and should be carefully examined rather than ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional events draw attention and may confirm, limit, or overthrow theories; historically, isolated anomalies (new stars, planetary irregularities) have spurred major advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify exceptional phenomena into eight kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Any supposed exception to known laws of nature can usually be referred to one of eight classes: (1) Imaginary/false; (2) Apparent but congruent; (3) Singular exceptions; (4) Divergent exceptions; (5) Accidental exceptions; (6) Novel and unexplained exceptions; (7) Limiting exceptions; (8) Contradictory/real exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to guide investigation and response. The text introduces and illustrates each category in succeeding sections; classification helps decide whether to disregard, reinterpret, restrict, or abandon a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginary (false) exceptions: investigate causes of false assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Imaginary or false exceptions are facts, objects, or events which are not really what they are supposed to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask how the false belief arose (mental conditions, careless assertion, careless acceptance). Verify claims experimentally and critically before building theoretical responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent but congruent exceptions: seek hidden agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions that seem to conflict with a law may in reality be in agreement with it (congruent exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for disguised forms or limits of detection (e.g., diffraction making light 'bend' subtly) that reconcile the phenomenon with the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular exceptions: rare unique results of a law
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular exceptions really agree with a law of nature but exhibit remarkable and unique results of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat them as special but lawful cases; study them for insight into boundary conditions or extreme manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent exceptions: excessive or monstrous results of known processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergent exceptions proceed from ordinary processes but are excessive in amount or monstrous in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether magnitude or scale differences account for apparent deviation and whether they suggest refinements in quantitative laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental exceptions: due to interference of a distinct known law
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidental exceptions arise from the interference of some entirely distinct but known law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the interfering cause; once accounted for, the original law may remain valid for the appropriate class of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel/unexplained exceptions: lead to discovery of new laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel and unexplained exceptions lead to the discovery of a new series of laws and phenomena, modifying or disguising effects of previously known laws without necessarily being inconsistent with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such exceptions as opportunities to expand theory; pursue further observation and theorizing to uncover underlying principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting exceptions: show falsity of overextended laws for some cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting exceptions show the falsity of a supposed law in some cases to which it had been extended, but do not affect its truth in other cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise the statement of the law to specify its proper domain; use exceptions to delimit classes for which the law holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictory/real exceptions: warrant abandoning a hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictory or real exceptions lead to the conclusion that a supposed hypothesis or theory is in opposition to the phenomena of nature and must therefore be abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an exception genuinely contradicts the applicable law and cannot be reconciled or reinterpreted, it may necessitate theory rejection or substantial revision.
